The issue here is a common design feature in modern power banks known as Auto-Shutoff or Low-Current Cutoff.

Most portable battery banks are designed to charge smartphones and tablets, which typically draw a significant amount of current ($500\text{ mA}$ to $2\text{ A}$ or more). When a device is fully charged, its current draw drops significantly. To save energy and prevent the battery bank's internal circuitry from draining itself, the bank detects this drop and shuts off the output.

Why it Shuts Off

A single USB LED typically draws a very low amount of current—often less than $50\text{ mA}$ to $100\text{ mA}$. Because this falls below the battery bank’s minimum threshold, the bank "thinks" nothing is connected or that the connected device is finished charging, so it kills the power after about 30 to 60 seconds.

Potential Solutions

  • Check for "Always-On" or "Low-Power" Mode: Many higher-end power banks (like those from Anker or Baseus) have a specific mode for low-power devices like Bluetooth headphones or LEDs.
    • The Trick: Try double-pressing or long-pressing the power button on the battery bank. If an LED indicator starts blinking or changes color, you may have successfully activated a low-current mode.
  • Add a Secondary Load: If the battery bank has a second USB port, try plugging in a more power-hungry device simultaneously (like your phone). The combined draw should keep the bank active, though this is obviously less efficient for just using a light.
  • Use a USB Dummy Load: There are inexpensive USB "keep-alive" or "dummy load" dongles designed specifically to pulse a small amount of current every few seconds to prevent the bank from sleeping.
  • Switch to a "Dumb" Power Source: A simple wall-wart USB charger or an older, less "smart" battery bank often won't have this auto-shutoff feature and will provide power indefinitely.

It appears the device is identifying the port types correctly, though a slight clarification on terminology may be useful for troubleshooting. The rectangular port commonly found on power banks is USB-A (the light itself has a USB-A connector), while USB-B is the square-shaped connector typically reserved for printers or older external hard drives.

Since the Heyday battery bank features both a USB-C and a USB-A port, there are two primary methods to keep the LED powered:

1. The "Parallel Load" Method

The most reliable way to bypass the auto-shutoff on a Heyday unit is to provide a larger power draw that the bank cannot ignore.

  • The Setup: Plug the LED into the USB-A port.
  • The Trigger: Plug a smartphone or another electronic device into the USB-C port.
  • The Result: The power bank will detect the phone's high current draw and keep the internal circuitry "awake," allowing the LED to remain lit simultaneously.

2. Testing for Low-Power Mode

While Heyday (a Target brand) typically produces straightforward "plug-and-play" devices without advanced features, some of their newer models have a hidden toggle.

  • Locate the power button on the side or face of the bank.
  • Try a quick double-press or a sustained 5-second hold.
  • If the LED status lights on the bank begin to "pulse" or cycle in a specific pattern, it may have entered a low-power mode designed for devices like headphones or small lights.

Why this is happening

Most power banks are programmed to "sleep" if the current draw drops below approximately 50 mA to 100 mA. A single LED often draws only 20 mA to 40 mA, which is essentially "invisible" to the battery bank's internal sensor.
